title: The plain (Luke 6:17–26)
hook: Luke's beatitudes: blessed are you poor, and woe to you who are rich
tomorrow: give, and it will be given

segments.voice: Yesterday, a whole night of prayer on the mountain before the twelve were chosen. Your line was pray first. Before your last real decision, did you stop for a minute of quiet? Day five hundred twenty-three.

In Matthew, the Beatitudes come from a mountain: Jesus goes up, sits down, and teaches. Luke tells it differently, and the difference starts with the ground. After the night of prayer, Jesus comes down with the twelve and "stood in the plain." The Greek means a level place. Not above the crowd. On the same ground as everyone. And the crowd is huge and mixed, from Judea and Jerusalem, and from the coast of Tyre and Sidon, outside Israel. People pushing forward to touch him, because, as Luke says, power was coming out of him and healing them all. Then he looks at his disciples, and starts to speak.

In the King James words: "Blessed be ye poor: for yours is the kingdom of God. Blessed are ye that hunger now: for ye shall be filled. Blessed are ye that weep now: for ye shall laugh." Notice three things. First, Luke's version says you. Blessed are you poor, not blessed are the poor in general. He's talking to the people in front of him, hungry ones, crying ones. Second, the word now. Hungry now, weeping now. This isn't the final word on their lives. Third, Matthew has blessed are the poor in spirit, and Luke has simply ye poor. Christians read the two side by side. Some stress actual poverty, as in the Catholic teaching sometimes called the preferential option for the poor; others stress the humble heart that knows it needs God. Then Luke does something Matthew doesn't. He turns the blessings over, and on the other side are woes. "But woe unto you that are rich! for ye have received your consolation. Woe unto you that are full! for ye shall hunger. Woe unto you that laugh now! for ye shall mourn and weep." Four blessings, four woes, like a coin with two faces. Woe in Greek is ouai, a cry rather than a curse; some readers hear it as alas, a warning said with sorrow. The blessed in Luke aren't the ones who seem to be winning. They're the hungry and the grieving, the ones on level ground. And the comfortable are warned, sadly, that comfort can become all the reward there is.
screen: then, large: `BLESSED BE YE POOR: FOR YOURS IS THE KINGDOM OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at who is blessed here. Settle, and breathe. Picture the level place, the crowd pressing in. Now picture your own neighborhood, your own commute. Who is hungry now? Who is weeping now? Who is the person people step around? Let a few faces come: the man outside the grocery store, the coworker who's been quiet since the funeral, the neighbor who's always short at the end of the month. In Luke, these are the ones Jesus calls blessed. Hold each face for a breath. Then ask, gently, which side of the coin you're on today, and what it would mean to stand on level ground with them. If you pray, you can hold them before God. If you don't, simply see them. The bell holds the time.
The plain. In Luke, Jesus teaches the Beatitudes on a level place, speaking to the poor, the hungry and the weeping as you, and adding four woes.
Your line: blessed are you poor. Today, look properly at one person most people overlook, learn their name if you can, and treat them as someone Jesus called blessed. Day five hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Christians often read Luke's Sermon on the Plain alongside Matthew's Sermon on the Mount, and some churches and charities draw on Luke 6:20–21 in their work with the poor and hungry.

match.prompt: what's inside Luke 6:17–26 — tap the pairs.
pairs: a level place, not a mountain
woe: alas, a cry of grief

myth: Luke's beatitudes say "blessed are the poor in spirit"
Luke says "blessed be ye poor"; "in spirit" is Matthew's wording.
Luke pairs the blessings with woes
in Luke, Jesus teaches from a mountaintop
he comes down and stands in the plain, a level place.

fork.setup: after a night of prayer on the mountain, you're about to teach a huge, mixed crowd. where do you stand?
options: stay up on the mountain where everyone can see.
come down and stand with them on a level place.
fork.reveal: Luke says he came down and stood in the plain, on the same ground as the crowd, and spoke to the poor as "you."

original.note: Greek: woe, alas. a cry of grief and warning, not a curse.

trapdoor: what you thought: Luke's beatitudes are Matthew's, shorter.
what it means: Luke's Jesus speaks straight to the poor, hungry and weeping as "you," and warns the rich, full and laughing with woes.
what a scholar hears: woe, ouai, is an exclamation close to alas, so some readers hear the woes as grief as much as threat.
recall: Latin for magnify, the song's first word

sources.quoted: Blessed be ye poor: for yours is the kingdom of God. Blessed are ye that hunger now: for ye shall be filled. Blessed are ye that weep now: for ye shall laugh.
But woe unto you that are rich! for ye have received your consolation. Woe unto you that are full! for ye shall hunger. Woe unto you that laugh now! for ye shall mourn and weep.

notes: 'Four blessings, four woes' counts 6:20–22 (poor, hungry, weeping, hated) and 6:24–26 (rich, full, laughing, spoken well of). Confirm.
'Preferential option for the poor' named as a Catholic social teaching phrase; the other reading (humble heart) described without ranking.
ouai as a lament or cry of grief: common lexicon note. Confirm.
